items.stem: Which is the definition of work done by a force?
options: Force × distance moved in any direction
Force × displacement in the direction of the force
items.answer: Force × displacement in the direction of the force
items.markingKey: W = Fs cos θ.

items.stem: Explain why a person holding a heavy suitcase at rest does no work on it.
items.answer: Work = force × displacement in the direction of the force; the suitcase does not move, so no work is done on it (although the muscles transfer energy internally).
items.markingKey: no displacement [1]; W = Fs = 0 [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the work done by the normal contact force on a box sliding along a horizontal floor is zero.
items.answer: The normal force is perpendicular to the displacement (θ = 90°, cos 90° = 0), so no work is done.
items.markingKey: perpendicular [1]; cos 90° = 0 [1] [2]

items.stem: A child pulls a sledge 2.0 m across snow with a rope held horizontally; the tension is 40 N. Determine the work done by the tension.
items.markingKey: W = Fs cos θ = 40 × 2.0 × cos 0° = 80 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A worker pulls a crate 3.5 m along a floor using a rope held parallel to the floor with a force of 80 N. A friction force of 48 N acts on the load. Calculate the work done by the tension, the work done against friction and the gain in kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: W_T = Fs cos θ = 280 J [1]; W_f = 48 × 3.5 = 168 J [1]; ΔKE = difference = 112 J [1] [3]

items.stem: A crate of mass 40 kg is pushed 5.0 m up a ramp inclined at 20° to the horizontal by a force of 400 N parallel to the ramp. A friction force of 80 N acts. (a) Calculate the work done by the pushing force. (b) Calculate the gain in kinetic energy. (c) Explain why the normal contact force does no work.
items.answer: (a) 2000 J (b) 929 J (c) It is perpendicular to the displacement.
items.markingKey: (a) W = Fs: 2000 J [1] (b) work-energy balance (method/substitution) [1]; answer 929 J with unit [1] [2] (c) It is perpendicular to the displacement [1]

items.stem: A force of 50 N pulls a box 4.0 m along the floor in the direction of the force. What work is done?
Explain why work done against friction results in an increase in thermal energy.
items.answer: The force does work over a displacement but the kinetic energy does not increase; the energy is transferred to internal (thermal) energy of the surfaces.
items.markingKey: work done against friction [1]; energy transferred to thermal energy of surfaces [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why it is easier to push a load up a long gentle ramp than to lift it straight up, although the work done against gravity is the same.
items.answer: The work mgh is the same, but over a longer distance a smaller force is needed (W = Fs).
items.markingKey: same work mgh [1]; longer distance, smaller force [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why it is easier to push a load up a long gentle ramp than to lift it straight up, although the work done against gravity is the same. (b) Explain why the work done by the normal contact force on a box sliding along a horizontal floor is zero.
items.answer: (a) The work mgh is the same, but over a longer distance a smaller force is needed (W = Fs). (b) The normal force is perpendicular to the displacement (θ = 90°, cos 90° = 0), so no work is done.
items.markingKey: (a) same work mgh [1]; longer distance, smaller force [1] [2] (b) perpendicular [1]; cos 90° = 0 [1] [2]

items.stem: The force on a trolley increases uniformly from 10 N to 50 N as it moves 0.50 m in the direction of the force. Calculate the work done, explaining how it is obtained from a force-displacement graph.
items.markingKey: work = area under F-s graph [1]; trapezium ½(10 + 50) × 0.50 [1]; = 15 J [1] [3]

items.stem: A tug pulls a barge 8.0 m with a cable at 45° to the direction of motion and tension 60 N. Determine the work done by the tension.
items.markingKey: W = Fs cos θ = 60 × 8.0 × cos 45° = 339 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A tug pulls a barge 3.5 m with a cable at 45° to the direction of motion and tension 150 N. A friction force of 63.6 N acts on the load. Calculate the work done by the tension, the work done against friction and the gain in kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: W_T = Fs cos θ = 371 J [1]; W_f = 63.6 × 3.5 = 223 J [1]; ΔKE = difference = 149 J [1]; justification via work-energy principle [1] [4]

items.stem: In a warehouse in Kuala Lumpur, a 80 kg box is pushed 8.0 m up a 20° slope with a force of 300 N along the slope against friction of 60 N. (a) Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy. (b) Calculate the work done against friction.
items.markingKey: (a) h = 8.0 sin 20° (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2150 J with unit [1] [2] (b) W = fs: 480 J [1]

items.stem: A crate of mass 40 kg is pushed 8.0 m up a ramp inclined at 20° to the horizontal by a force of 400 N parallel to the ramp. A friction force of 80 N acts. (a) Calculate the work done by the pushing force. (b) Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy. (c) Calculate the work done against friction.
items.markingKey: (a) W = Fs: 3200 J [1] (b) h = 8.0 sin 20° (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1070 J with unit [1] [2] (c) W = fs: 640 J [1]

items.stem: A 2.0 kg mass is raised through 3.0 m. What is its gain in gravitational potential energy?
Derive the equation E_k = ½mv² for a body accelerated from rest by a constant force.
items.answer: Work done W = Fs = (ma)s; with v² = 2as from rest, as = v²/2; so W = m(v²/2) = ½mv², which becomes kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: W = Fs = mas [1]; v² = 2as [1]; substitution gives ½mv² [1] [3]

items.stem: Derive ΔE_p = mgΔh for an object lifted at constant speed.
items.answer: The lifting force equals the weight mg; work done = force × distance = mgΔh, which is stored as gravitational potential energy.
items.markingKey: force = mg at constant speed [1]; W = mgΔh [1] [2]

items.stem: A sledge and rider of total mass 75 kg slide from rest down a hill with a vertical drop of 12 m. Resistive forces are negligible. Determine the speed at the bottom.
items.markingKey: mgh = ½mv² → v = √(2 × 9.81 × 12) = 15.3 m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A ball of mass 0.20 kg falls from rest through 4.0 m. 25% of the potential energy lost is transferred to thermal energy by resistive forces. Calculate its speed at the bottom.

A roller-coaster car of mass 500 kg descends a vertical height of 4.0 m from rest along a path of length 30 m and reaches a speed of 7.41 m s⁻¹. (a) Calculate the loss of gravitational potential energy. (b) Calculate the kinetic energy at the bottom. (c) Calculate the average resistive force along the path.
Nadia drops a 0.20 kg rubber ball from 1.2 m; it bounces back up to 0.84 m. (a) Calculate the speed just before impact. (b) Calculate the kinetic energy lost in the bounce.
items.markingKey: (a) v = √(2gh) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.85 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) mg(h − h_b) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.706 J with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Amara drops a 0.20 kg rubber ball from 1.8 m; it bounces back up to 1.44 m. (a) Calculate the speed just before impact. (b) Calculate the kinetic energy lost in the bounce. (c) State and explain whether the bounce is elastic.
items.answer: (a) 5.94 m s⁻¹ (b) 0.706 J (c) Inelastic: kinetic energy is lost (rebound height is less).
items.markingKey: (a) v = √(2gh) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5.94 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) mg(h − h_b) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.706 J with unit [1] [2] (c) Inelastic: kinetic energy is lost (rebound height is less) [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) The equation ΔE = mgΔh is valid … (b) What is the kinetic energy of a 0.50 kg ball moving at 4.0 m s⁻¹?
items.answer: (a) only for small changes in height near the Earth's surface where g is constant (b) 4.0 J
items.markingKey: (a) It assumes a uniform gravitational field. (b) E = ½mv² = 0.5 × 0.50 × 16.

items.stem: Explain why a pendulum bob swinging in air eventually stops.
items.answer: Work is done against air resistance (and friction at the pivot), so the mechanical energy is gradually transferred to thermal energy of the surroundings.
items.markingKey: work against air resistance/friction [1]; energy transferred to thermal [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a ball dropped from a height h reaches the same speed whatever its mass, if air resistance is negligible.
items.answer: mgh = ½mv², and m cancels, so v = √(2gh) is independent of mass.
items.markingKey: energy equation [1]; mass cancels [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why a ball dropped from a height h reaches the same speed whatever its mass, if air resistance is negligible. (b) Explain why a pendulum bob swinging in air eventually stops.
items.answer: (a) mgh = ½mv², and m cancels, so v = √(2gh) is independent of mass. (b) Work is done against air resistance (and friction at the pivot), so the mechanical energy is gradually transferred to thermal energy of the surroundings.
items.markingKey: (a) energy equation [1]; mass cancels [1] [2] (b) work against air resistance/friction [1]; energy transferred to thermal [1] [2]

items.answer: (a) mgh = ½mv², and m cancels, so v = √(2gh) is independent of mass. (b) Work done W = Fs = (ma)s; with v² = 2as from rest, as = v²/2; so W = m(v²/2) = ½mv², which becomes kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: (a) energy equation [1]; mass cancels [1] [2] (b) W = Fs = mas [1]; v² = 2as [1]; substitution gives ½mv² [1] [3]

items.stem: A roller-coaster car of mass 400 kg descends a vertical height of 12 m from rest. Resistive forces are negligible. What is the speed at the bottom?

A ball of mass 0.15 kg is thrown from the top of a building 15 m high with a speed of 8.0 m s⁻¹. Use energy considerations to calculate its speed just before it hits the ground, ignoring air resistance. Explain why the direction of the throw does not matter.
items.answer: 18.9 m s⁻¹; energy is a scalar, so the final kinetic energy depends only on initial KE and height lost.
items.markingKey: ½mu² + mgh = ½mv² [1]; v = √(8.0² + 2 × 9.81 × 15) = 18.9 m s⁻¹ [1]; energy is scalar / independent of direction [1] [3]

items.stem: A sledge and rider of total mass 50 kg slide from rest down a hill with a vertical drop of 1.5 m. Resistive forces are negligible. Calculate the speed at the bottom.

items.stem: A ball of mass 0.15 kg is thrown from the top of a building 5.0 m high with a speed of 15 m s⁻¹. Use energy considerations to calculate its speed just before it hits the ground, ignoring air resistance. Explain why the direction of the throw does not matter.
items.answer: 18.0 m s⁻¹; energy is a scalar, so the final kinetic energy depends only on initial KE and height lost.
items.markingKey: ½mu² + mgh = ½mv² [1]; v = √(15² + 2 × 9.81 × 5.0) = 18.0 m s⁻¹ [1]; energy is scalar / independent of direction [1] [3]

items.answer: (a) 7.00 m s⁻¹ (b) work = force × distance = mg × Δh
items.markingKey: (a) v = √(2gh) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 7.00 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) force mg [1]; × Δh [1] [2]

items.stem: Elena drops a 0.050 kg rubber ball from 1.2 m; it bounces back up to 0.72 m. (a) Calculate the speed just before impact. (b) Calculate the kinetic energy lost in the bounce. (c) Derive the expression for gravitational potential energy change ΔE = mgΔh.
items.answer: (a) 4.85 m s⁻¹ (b) 0.235 J (c) work = force × distance = mg × Δh
items.markingKey: (a) v = √(2gh) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.85 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) mg(h − h_b) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.235 J with unit [1] [2] (c) force mg [1]; × Δh [1] [2]

items.stem: A gas expands at constant pressure p from volume V₁ to V₂. What work does it do?
items.markingKey: W = pΔV at constant pressure.

items.stem: A gas at 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa expands by 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ at constant pressure. What work is done by the gas?
Derive W = pΔV for a gas pushing a piston of area A through a distance Δx.
items.answer: Force on piston F = pA; work = FΔx = pAΔx = pΔV since AΔx = ΔV.
items.markingKey: F = pA [1]; W = pAΔx = pΔV [1] [2]

items.stem: Gas in a cylinder at a constant pressure of 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa expands from 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³, pushing a piston. Determine the work done by the gas.
items.markingKey: W = pΔV = 1.5 × 10⁵ × 1.0 × 10⁻³ = 150 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The gas in a balloon-type actuator expands by 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³ at a constant 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa when 150 J of heat is supplied. (a) Calculate the work done by the gas. (b) State what would happen to the work done if the same expansion occurred at twice the pressure.
items.markingKey: (a) W = pΔV (method/substitution) [1]; answer 90.0 J with unit [1] [2] (b) It would double [1]

items.stem: On a graph of pressure against volume, the work done by a gas is represented by …
options: the product of the final pressure and volume
the intercept on the pressure axis
items.markingKey: W = ∫p dV.

items.stem: Explain why a gas expanding against a piston does work.
items.answer: The gas exerts a force on the piston (pressure × area) and the piston moves in the direction of that force, so work is done by the gas.
items.markingKey: force from pressure on piston [1]; displacement in direction of force [1] [2]

items.stem: The gas in an engine cylinder at a constant 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa increases in volume from 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³ to 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³. What is the work done by the gas?
Air in a syringe is heated and expands at constant pressure 2.5 × 10⁵ Pa from 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³. Work out the work done by the gas.
items.markingKey: W = pΔV = 2.5 × 10⁵ × 1.5 × 10⁻³ = 375 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The gas in an engine cylinder at a constant 2.5 × 10⁵ Pa increases in volume from 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 4.5 × 10⁻³ m³. The piston has area 5.0 × 10⁻³ m². Calculate the work done by the gas, the force on the piston and the distance the piston moves. Show that your answers are consistent.
Which is the definition of power?
items.markingKey: P = W/t.

items.stem: Derive P = Fv from the definition of power.
items.answer: P = W/t = Fs/t = F(s/t) = Fv, for a constant force in the direction of motion at velocity v.
items.markingKey: P = W/t and W = Fs [1]; s/t = v [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why no machine can have an efficiency greater than 100%.
items.answer: Energy is conserved, so the useful output energy cannot exceed the input; some energy is always transferred to wasted forms (e.g. thermal) by friction.
items.markingKey: conservation of energy [1]; output ≤ input, always some loss [1] [2]

items.stem: A car travels at a constant 30 m s⁻¹ along a level road. The total resistive force is 1500 N. Work out the output power of the engine.
items.markingKey: P = Fv = 1500 × 30 = 45 000 W. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A pump raises water through a vertical height of 15 m at a rate of 2.0 kg s⁻¹. The water leaves the pipe at 5.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the minimum power output of the pump, taking into account the kinetic energy given to the water.
items.markingKey: GPE per second = 294 W [1]; KE per second = ½ × 2.0 × 5.0² = 25 W [1]; total = 319 W [1] [3]

items.stem: An athlete of mass 70 kg climbs a staircase rising 4.0 m in 5.0 s during a fitness test. (a) Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy. (b) The body converts chemical energy with an efficiency of 20%. Calculate the rate of chemical energy use. (c) Define efficiency.
items.answer: (a) 2750 J (b) 2750 W (c) useful energy (or power) output ÷ total energy (or power) input
items.markingKey: (a) mgh: 2750 J [1] (b) P_in = P_out/η (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2750 W with unit [1] [2] (c) useful energy (or power) output ÷ total energy (or power) input [1]

items.stem: A car moves at a constant 25 m s⁻¹ against a resistive force of 800 N. What useful power does the engine deliver?
Explain why a car needs more power to travel at a constant high speed than at a constant low speed.
items.answer: At constant speed driving force = resistive force, which increases with speed; P = Fv increases because both F and v are larger.
items.markingKey: resistive force increases with v [1]; P = Fv so increases [1] [2]

items.stem: Two cranes lift identical loads to the same height, one in half the time. Compare the work done and the power.
items.answer: Same work done (mgh) but the faster crane has twice the power (P = W/t).
items.markingKey: same work [1]; double power [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Derive P = Fv from the definition of power. (b) Two cranes lift identical loads to the same height, one in half the time. Compare the work done and the power.

items.answer: p is not constant; the work must be found from the area under the p-V graph instead.

items.stem: Gas in a cylinder at a constant pressure of 2.5 × 10⁵ Pa expands from 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 4.5 × 10⁻³ m³, pushing a piston. Determine the work done by the gas.
items.markingKey: W = pΔV = 2.5 × 10⁵ × 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 125 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Derive P = Fv from the definition of power. (b) Two cranes lift identical loads to the same height, one in half the time. Compare the work done and the power.
items.answer: (a) P = W/t = Fs/t = F(s/t) = Fv, for a constant force in the direction of motion at velocity v. (b) Same work done (mgh) but the faster crane has twice the power (P = W/t).
items.markingKey: (a) P = W/t and W = Fs [1]; s/t = v [1] [2] (b) same work [1]; double power [1] [2]

items.stem: A boat moves at constant speed through calm water. The resistive force is tripled while the speed stays the same. State and explain how the useful power needed changes.
items.markingKey: Using P = Fv: useful power needed ∝ resistive force; factor = 3.00 = 3.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A pump raises water through a vertical height of 10 m at a rate of 5.0 kg s⁻¹. Work out the useful power output.
items.markingKey: P = (m/t)gh = 5.0 × 9.81 × 10 = 491 W. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A car travels at a constant 25 m s⁻¹ along a level road. The total resistive force is 1200 N. The engine can deliver a maximum power of 60 000 W and the car has mass 1000 kg. Calculate the power needed at 25 m s⁻¹ and the maximum possible acceleration at this speed.
items.markingKey: P = Fv = 30 000 W [1]; max driving force = P_max/v = 2400 N [1]; resultant = 1200 N [1]; a = 1.2 m s⁻² [1] [4]

items.stem: An athlete of mass 70 kg climbs a staircase rising 4.5 m in 3.0 s during a fitness test. (a) Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy. (b) The body converts chemical energy with an efficiency of 25%. Calculate the rate of chemical energy use. (c) Define efficiency. (d) Suggest why the measured power is an underestimate of the power actually developed.
items.answer: (a) 3090 J (b) 4120 W (c) useful energy (or power) output ÷ total energy (or power) input (d) Energy is also transferred to kinetic energy and thermal energy, and the arms/legs move; only mgh is counted.
items.markingKey: (a) mgh: 3090 J [1] (b) P_in = P_out/η (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4120 W with unit [1] [2] (c) useful energy (or power) output ÷ total energy (or power) input [1] (d) Energy is also transferred to kinetic energy and thermal energy, and the arms/legs move; only mgh is counted [1]

items.stem: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at constant speed. How much work does gravity do on it?
items.markingKey: The gravitational force is perpendicular to the motion.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the work done by the normal contact force on a box sliding along a horizontal floor is zero. (b) Explain why a person holding a heavy suitcase at rest does no work on it.
items.answer: (a) The normal force is perpendicular to the displacement (θ = 90°, cos 90° = 0), so no work is done. (b) Work = force × displacement in the direction of the force; the suitcase does not move, so no work is done on it (although the muscles transfer energy internally).
items.markingKey: (a) perpendicular [1]; cos 90° = 0 [1] [2] (b) no displacement [1]; W = Fs = 0 [1] [2]

items.stem: The force on a trolley increases uniformly from 30 N to 50 N as it moves 2.0 m in the direction of the force. Calculate the work done, explaining how it is obtained from a force-displacement graph.
items.markingKey: work = area under F-s graph [1]; trapezium ½(30 + 50) × 2.0 [1]; = 80 J [1] [3]

items.stem: A worker pulls a crate 8.0 m along a floor using a rope at 45° to the floor with a force of 30 N. A friction force of 12.7 N acts on the load. Calculate the work done by the tension, the work done against friction and the gain in kinetic energy.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Derive ΔE_p = mgΔh for an object lifted at constant speed. (b) Explain why a ball dropped from a height h reaches the same speed whatever its mass, if air resistance is negligible.
items.answer: (a) The lifting force equals the weight mg; work done = force × distance = mgΔh, which is stored as gravitational potential energy. (b) mgh = ½mv², and m cancels, so v = √(2gh) is independent of mass.
items.markingKey: (a) force = mg at constant speed [1]; W = mgΔh [1] [2] (b) energy equation [1]; mass cancels [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why a pendulum bob swinging in air eventually stops. (b) Derive ΔE_p = mgΔh for an object lifted at constant speed.
items.answer: (a) Work is done against air resistance (and friction at the pivot), so the mechanical energy is gradually transferred to thermal energy of the surroundings. (b) The lifting force equals the weight mg; work done = force × distance = mgΔh, which is stored as gravitational potential energy.
items.markingKey: (a) work against air resistance/friction [1]; energy transferred to thermal [1] [2] (b) force = mg at constant speed [1]; W = mgΔh [1] [2]

items.stem: A roller-coaster car of mass 650 kg descends a vertical height of 8.0 m from rest. Resistive forces are negligible. Work out the speed at the bottom.
items.markingKey: mgh = ½mv² → v = √(2 × 9.81 × 8.0) = 12.5 m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A ball of mass 0.20 kg is thrown from the top of a building 15 m high with a speed of 20 m s⁻¹. Use energy considerations to calculate its speed just before it hits the ground, ignoring air resistance. Explain why the direction of the throw does not matter.
items.answer: 26.3 m s⁻¹; energy is a scalar, so the final kinetic energy depends only on initial KE and height lost.
items.markingKey: ½mu² + mgh = ½mv² [1]; v = √(20² + 2 × 9.81 × 15) = 26.3 m s⁻¹ [1]; energy is scalar / independent of direction [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a gas expanding against a piston does work. (b) Explain why W = pΔV cannot be used directly for a gas whose pressure changes during expansion.
items.answer: (a) The gas exerts a force on the piston (pressure × area) and the piston moves in the direction of that force, so work is done by the gas. (b) p is not constant; the work must be found from the area under the p-V graph instead.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Two cranes lift identical loads to the same height, one in half the time. Compare the work done and the power. (b) Explain why no machine can have an efficiency greater than 100%.
items.answer: (a) Same work done (mgh) but the faster crane has twice the power (P = W/t). (b) Energy is conserved, so the useful output energy cannot exceed the input; some energy is always transferred to wasted forms (e.g. thermal) by friction.
items.markingKey: (a) same work [1]; double power [1] [2] (b) conservation of energy [1]; output ≤ input, always some loss [1] [2]
